doctrine. But Christ did not teach contradictory doc-
trines. Again, in this same parable, he says

ified by the members of the human body? No, my brethren; and

form a universal church, however different their
belief and modes of discipline? This, my brethren,
is a common remark and is also the mark of all the in-
differentism which overspreads the land. Let
us say little on it. We know that the United States and Eng-

constitute but one kingdom? You all know that they

I must finish what I have to say on the worms and introduce the insect and crustacea; I shall avoid repeating what I said in the last lecture and proceed at once to the remaining types in the class of worms. The families which we have discussed are the lowest—those without any external appendages, provided only with transverse articulations or rings. The other worms are not parasitic; at least few of them are, and most of them have shorter bodies composed of fewer rings than the intestinal worms. In one of the families which I have received the name of Apoda, and contains a great number of fresh-water worms, we have that extraordinary type in which the alimentary canal is branched like blood-vessels; it is very beautiful to sight to see through the transparent body, the alimentary canal branching like a blood-vessel, contracting and expanding, and the alimentary fluid running through the vessels like blood, to the periphery. THIS WAY THEY PULLED THEM UP, AND LET
HIM FALL. The following amusing adventure,
given by correspondent, writing from Buffalo,
actually took place in the town of NJ, in Ohio,
two years ago. It would have made the late
Isaac Hicks, laugh at a solemn "Seventh day"
meeting. The farmer had two daughters, very
interesting young ladies, ye, in their teens, who
were quite romantic in their notions. Their
father was an aristocratic member of the Baptist
church, and of course was very particular as to
what company his girls should keep. Now it
happened this, these two girls became acquaint-
ed with a couple of young bucks, clerks in an
adjoining village, and, to use common phrase,

took quite a shine to them. To this the old
gentleman was very much opposed, as it in-
tended to match his daughters himself. But
it was no use talking to them; while week after
week wore away, and found the young men
constant visitors. At length, in order to en-
force obedience the old man found himself dri-
ven to the necessity of locking up his foolish
children, who had presumed without his consent
to fall in love with a couple of poor tradesmen.
The sweet girls were accordingly confined on

Sunday afternoons in the back bedroom in the
second story, which fronted the barnyard with a
very romantic look out. Under the window was
a pile of stones which had been left after re-
pairing the cellar-wall in that corner. For two
or three successive Sabbath evenings, the usu-
al period of visiting their paramours, the lovers
had climbed, by means of the sheets of the bed,
which were let down from the window by the
heroic girls, up to the apartment of their impr-
isoned lovers, and from nightfall until rosy morn-
ing did revel in the ambrosial delights of love's
young dreams. But this clandestine courtship
could not be continued without being at last di-
scovered. One lovely Sabbath just at twilight,
the father coming from the barn thought he saw
some rather ominous hanging out of the back
window; so walked noiselessly around to ascer-
tain the nature of it. There hung the fatal
flag of surrender and the old man giving it a
slight jerk, commenced the ascent. He was
lifted gently from off his feet, and felt himself

the new regiment of Tennessee volunteers, which embark-
ed here days ago under the command of Col. Cheatham, is a body of troops whose appearance and state of
discipline can hardly be exceeded. The individuals
composing it are of them in comfortable circumstances,
and have joined the regiment impelled solely by desire
to serve their country and advance the honor of her.

consequently from their infancy familiar with the use of the
rifle. It would be difficult for an equal number of any

distance.

Cheatham's regiment—not for the purpose of claiming
priority for it, but rather to exhibit a specimen of the
materials which compose our whole army in Mexico.

Queretaro, the place to which the Mexicans have transferred the seat of government, is a fine town or city of some thirty-five thousand inhabitants, noted, and distinguished for its manufactures, particularly of coarse woolens and cottons. It is about one hundred and twenty miles W. of Mexico, and is seated on the borders of the Mexican—a great mountain plain or valley, of some two thousand feet less elevated than the valley of Mexico, which stretches sixty or more miles wide, to the neighborhood of the larger city of Guanajuato, and is considered the richest, as it is, in fact, the most fertile tract of land in Mexico. The whole of this country, with its vicinity, is densely peopled. The state of Guanajuato, with a territory considerably less than that of Massachusetts, has a population of upwards of half a million. The state of Queretaro, which is twice as large, contains a population variously estimated from one hundred and twenty-five up to five hundred thousand souls—a remarkable example of the uncertainty that exists, in Mexico, in regard to most important points of national statistics, which are all guessed at.

Queretaro is, then, the new seat of Gov.
Pena y Pena, once strong friend of peace, now an ardent advocate of war, attended by General President Herrera, another convert from peace to war, convokes the Mexican congress, from which there is perhaps as little to be expected of pacific inclination as from the administration of the peace President.

And in the meanwhile, will he succeed in this ill-conceived enterprise? Santa Anna, always defeated and never subdued, remains in the rear, raising new armies to fight new battles—or so destroy convoys and caissons, and perhaps reconquer undecided territories.

Santa Anna appears to be, in fact, the war-hero; his admission into Mexico aroused a war spirit which did not previously exist. With all his faults, and all our ideas of his unpopularity, he is the next and most popular and influential of all the Mexican chiefs, and is the rallying point of the Mexican people. He dares not make peace, and war is the state of things in which he is most powerful, by being most necessary to his country. The best way to end the war would be to capture him, if possible, or expel him from the country. It was a cardinal principle of the old Romans to pursue a defeated enemy until he was in their power, or driven away a powerless fugitive far from the theatre of conflict.

Benton's Decision.

It has already been stated that Mr. Benton has declined the appointment of Major General in the army. There has been a great deal of speculation in the newspapers and elsewhere regarding to this matter. The following correspondences will set the whole of it satisfactorily before the public.

Letter from Mr. Benton to the President

Washington, March 9, 1847.

SIR—Without waiting for the formality of being presented with the commission of Major General in the army of the United States, I think it right to inform you, once, that my acceptance or refusal of that high appointment, will depend entirely upon public and national considerations of which you, YOURSELF will be the judge. Personally I can have no wish for this office, but if you believe that I can be of service to the country, I am willing to forgo all private considerations—separate myself from my family, under painful circumstances, resign my place in the Senate, which is so dear to me, and proceed immediately to the theatre of war. My only stipulation would be for the powers which I deem necessary to success! and these would be both military and diplomatic—the command of the army and authority to sign preliminaries of peace, based upon terms previously approved by you. I hope you will believe, sir, that nothing is selfish of personal dictates in this proposed situation. There is no such thing in it. It proceeds from thorough conviction that, with subordinate command, I could do no good in the army; on the contrary, that my presence there would be improper and mischievous; for I am known from my public speeches, to disapprove the plans, both of the late and of the present commander—his defensive policy of one and the San Luis of Ulua attack of the other; and this being known, my presence would open up an implied censure on the two generals, and might make me, in spite of myself, the nucleus of discontent and insubordination. The command of the army, therefore, is the only military position which could hold it. I deem highly essential to success, authority to conclude peace, or at least to sign the preliminaries of peace. I deem highly essential to success, as it would enable this Commander-in-chief to take instant advantage of all passing events, military or political, to close the war.

Furnished with these powers, I am willing to make the sacrifices, and to incur the responsibilities of this command; but leave it to you, sir, for your free and fast decision considering the national question, and a new one, on which there is no commitment, on either side, in anything that has passed.

Whatevers may be the decision, my thanks and gratitude will not be the less to you for your unsolicited nomination of me to the high appointment, nor to the Senate for its instant and unanimous confirmation of it, nor to the House of Representatives for its three times virtual election of me to be the commander in chief of the army in Mexico.

Few of our readers acquainted with the extent of the iron business in Tennessee. Mr. Morean, in his report to the Legislature, estimates the capital employed in the business at $1,500,000, and the annual products at the same amount. Three fourths of this capital is employed in Middle Tennessee and would contribute to the support of the Nashville and Chattanooga railroad. On the Cumberland river, near Nashville there are blast furnaces, forges, and splendid rolling mills which yield annually about $4,000. On the Tennessee river, there are 11 furnaces and forges and bloomeries, which produce about 150,000 tons annually. East Tennessee is particularly rich in iron ore, water power and fuel of every kind. At present the products of their mines and furnaces are carried down the Tennessee, the Gle shoals, thence to the Ohio and up that river to Pittsburgh, where they manufacture and are returned to the South for consumption. At Chattanooga iron is purchased for $3 per ton, while it commands in Savannah something like $8. The moment the Georgia improvements reach the Tennessee, the whole trade of the country bordering upon that river, its tributaries above Chattanooga, will be directed towards the Atlantic. The iron, the corn, the flour, the fruit, the tobacco, the hemp, and the thousand other products of that region will swell the trade of State works to at least double, perhaps tenfold, what it is at present. Iron, for instance, could then be brought from Chattanooga to Macon, commissions included, for about the same freight now paid from Savannah, say 30 cents per cwt, which would give it to the people of Macon and the planters of middle Georgia a little two thirds the price now paid.

According to an able letter addressed by J. S. T. Yenson, Esq to the Hon. John G. Calhoun, we are surprised to learn that the agricultural products of Tennessee in value equal $50,550, while those of Ohio only $150,391 and of New York $65,400, showing Tennessee to be the third State in the Union in productive wealth. According to the same authority the annual value of all kinds of agricultural and manufactured articles produced in the immediate vicinity of the proposed railroad between Chattanooga and Nashville amounts to $12,642,540. And yet the items enumerated by Mr. S. has entirely omitted the article of wheat, of which Tennessee produces 40,000 bushels per year, nearly one half of which grown in the Cumberland valley.

Macon Journal and Messenger

NEW YORK, July 1877.
THE EDITOR OF THE TRIBUNE:


In The Sun of this day is published an Editorial article under the heading Of Cuba under the Flag Of the United States, which has aroused the attention Of all who feel an interest in that Island, from the extravaganza Of its conception and the unbounded assertions which it contains. The Editor says that he took part in a meeting Of the most influential and wealthy citizens Of Havana, on the subject Of the annexation Of Cuba to the United States and that he promised to bring the subject fully before the people Of this country there should be a settlement Of the Mexican question. Here is the first which claims correction. The persons of the class referred to neither hold, have held meetings Of such description. True is that singular coincidence brought into connection two remarkable events which are well worthy Of the serious consideration Of the Spanish Government and which have probably given rise to the conjectures for which alone can they be called Of the Editor Of The Sun. These two events are, let us say, the Military and Religious System which the past eleven years have established in Cuba and, in The policy of the United States which is characterized by thirst Of dominion and territorial extension. True it is, that in these latter days, since the momentous hour when the deputies Of

Cuba assert that Island essentially a country Of productive industry, hostile abrupt changes and alien to political institutions has seen torn from it day after day and by one all the guarantees which for three centuries had been preserved to the Queen Of the Antilles By the laws, the habits of the country ever since the Conquest and the interests Of the Spanish Crown. Its government being committed to the hands Of Spanish generals and a host of officials in effect wholly irresponsible, while they have constantly alleged dread Of political disturbances for pretended strict adherence to the established system Of Administration and for turning a deaf ear to every suggestion Of liberal improvement, they have in fact pursued precisely the opposite course and themselves Introduced the most radical changes subversive Of all popular rights and Of the most cherished customs and time-honored institutions Of the Island. The Municipalities (Ayuntamientos) and the Consulado Council Of improvement (Junta de Fomento) to whose energetic voice used to reach, and with influential effect the ears Of the Sovereign, have been so modified in their organization and attributes to constitute merely ridiculous pedestals on which is planted with firmer security, the military power curiously formalized with the entire body of civil officials. The Royal Courts (Audiencias) whose magistrates were in other days the honor and pride Of the Spanish nation, tempering and correcting the excuses Of the military authority, have also bent the neck before that Colossus whose career has been like that Of a mighty torrent which oversteps the last restraint upon its ever increasing impetus, and threatens general foundation.

It is undeniable that at a period like the present, and when there is a natural consequence Of such radical want of order and harmony, the wealth Of the Island have found themselves embarrassed by the Oppressions Of a prohibitory system devised by the mer-

there is nothing strange in the supposition Of deep discontent on part of the property Of Cuba when they, the producers Of its annual riches, behold few privileged provinces Of Spain and most of others on the same footing, the ever increasing impositions direct and indirect, public and private, At their own simple caprice; and when they behold the plea of want Of authority advanced only when some measure of relief to the public burdens is proposed. (As occurred during the surprises caused by the late hurricanes), the injuries inflicted on property could not but have excited painful reflections, and bitter comparisons between the present and the past. But all this is very distant from the statement of the editor of The Sun.

That the geographical position and other advantages Of that invaluable Island may MAKE IT an OBJECT of desire to the American Union, can very readily be conceived; but to suppose its Inhabitants to be in a state Of effervescence and agitation and clamoring for entrance INTO this Union in disregard of their ancient customs and At the risk of fatal consequences, and engaged in plotting conspiracies, is not only false but very insulting in regard to the inhabitants of the Island, who lament there the expressions they suffer and against whom will be made imputations founded perhaps on this article of The Sun.

This is saying that the property of Cuba is sensitive to the injuries inflicted by the new system of military government which has been brought into existence there; it is not saying that the destruction Of all its rights and securities is beheld with Indifference; but there probably is not In the whole world community more discreet and alive To what is required by their interest, the proprietors Of the Island Of Cuba. They would, it is true, desire to restrain this oppressive course—the more deeply felt from its wide contrast with the favorable regards they considered to merit from the hand of the late monarch. They would desire TO be secure against Illegal prosecutions, capricious taxation and personal oppression. They would desire no longer to behold their sons, now they in effect behold them excluded, for the crime Of birth in the American hemisphere, from all the employments which are paid by their industry. They would desire that the public mind might enjoy the freedom necessary TO permit the opinion of the country to be disregarded when its material interests are concerned. They would desire TO behold the doors Of the public corporations no longer in effect closed against their men Of the most illustrious reputation. They would desire that the law of residence, of the guarantees Of the Laws of the land, now in disuse, whatever refers to the rights Of the Commons, should not be a mere vain and illusory form. They would desire, in fine, that Spain, which was a model of mildness in the administration Of the Island, especially within the last century, now when other nations profiting by her teachings are opening a liberal hand for colonial concessions, should not undertake the opposite course of establishing commercial and political restrictions, each one and more foreign to the intelligence which surrounds us, and Incompatible with the lights and progress of the age. The principles Of the League, directed in England by the immortal Golden Rule, and which have been reached and understood by the enlightened classes of Havana, may have tended, it is true, to create an indifference to the nationality Of countries; but from the same Cause results also the consequence that the franchises Of liberal political economy are the object of universal desire. Already In Spain the voice of the great principle Of the Freedom of Trade has been allowed to be heard. The Inhabitants Of Cuba do not need to be taught the rapidity with which these Principles make their mark, which are at once comprehended and applauded by all the world; and consequently, as soon as they behold them there dawning above the peninsular horizon, the nearing hope is strengthened Of seeing them soon diffusing themselves like the rays Of a

benevolent and formulating sun, over all the dominions of Spain. The inhabitants Of Cuba are ever engaged IN extensive enterprise, and they have a vast commerce founded On their immense annual agricultural production, of not less than fifty millions of dollars, including the consumption Of the country. To be endangered by launching into the career Of political vicissitudes, a single bad crop, interruption Of commerce for a few months, or any other cause of instability, might involve consequences that would be tremendous and Thousand fold in their results than the evils which are now with Justice lamented. Those industrious members Of the Spanish family have as natural a strong attachment to their old habits, to their prejudices, and even to all the present infections they suffer, as they have NOT been able to erase from their memory the benefits she bestowed upon them from the generous hand of the last King, the father Of the young Queen now on the throne Of Spain.
